course.title: Notes that do work

featuredImage.caption: Raw notes become linked ideas, a decision brief and a handover.

course.description: Turn scattered reading, meeting notes and half-formed ideas into decisions, drafts and handovers you can use again. You will build the system around one real question, give AI only the checked context it needs, and review its answer before it joins your notes. Obsidian is one example, not a requirement.
course.audience: Professionals whose useful thinking is spread across notebooks, documents, email, meeting records and note apps. You need one real, low-risk question to work on and somewhere you can write and search. You may use an approved AI tool, but the course also works with a synthetic example. You do not need Obsidian, a database, a special folder structure, coding skills or a large archive of existing notes.
course.outcome: You finish with a small working knowledge system built around a real question, a checked source pack for AI-assisted work, a source-backed brief another person can use, and a handover that records what should be checked or reused next time.

sections.title: Capture with a purpose
sections.outcome: Find one place where useful thinking disappears, then turn a real capture into a source note you can trust later.

lessons.title: Find where useful thinking disappears
lessons.outcome: Choose one live work question, trace where its useful context currently sits, and name the exact point where that context becomes hard to find or reuse.
lessons.exercise: Choose one low-risk question you need to answer in the next fortnight. Trace the notes, sources, messages and prior work you would use, then mark the point where useful context is most likely to disappear before the next related job.

artifact.description: A map of one real work question, the places its useful context currently lives, who needs the eventual output, and the single leak you will repair during the course.

verification: The question is real, bounded and safe to use for practice.
Each source location names an actual notebook, folder, app, document or person rather than a category such as information.
The leak identifies where context becomes hard to find, interpret or reuse rather than blaming the tool in general.
The map names the reader and the decision, action or handover the eventual output must support.
You have chosen one leak to repair instead of proposing to reorganise everything.

content.text: Outcome
Find one place where useful thinking from your work disappears, and pick the question you will carry through the rest of the course.
Before you continue

Do not read on yet. Write down one question you need to answer in the next fortnight. Without searching, list every place you think the relevant context lives. Circle the place you would least like a colleague to inherit tomorrow.
See it

An accountant is preparing a month-end review. Three variances in a spreadsheet are still unexplained. The reason for one of them is in an email, a correction came up in a meeting, and a handwritten reminder mentions a late invoice. The review itself may be accurate. When the spreadsheet is filed, though, most of the thinking that made it accurate goes with it, and next month begins with the same search.

The accountant did take notes. The reasons, sources and decisions just ended up separated from the work they explained. Call that separation a leak: the point where useful context stops being available to the next person, or to the next version of you. It can open at capture, when a note has no source; during use, when nobody records why a decision was made; or at handover, when the useful reasoning stays inside a finished document nobody searches.

Which of those matters depends on the job in front of you, so begin with the question you actually have to answer. That question tells you which context deserves to survive. It also keeps you off the detour where a weekend goes into naming folders and Monday's question is still unanswered.
Choose a surface you can already use
You need somewhere you can write and search text, then link or refer to another note. Use an approved tool you already have. These official guides show the minimum moves in four common surfaces:
Obsidian Help
OneNote for Windows: basic tasks
Notion: links and backlinks
Apple Notes: add links

attrs.alt: Obsidian's desktop app showing a note, folder and note lists, and a graph view, with a mobile note beside it.
attrs.title: An official Obsidian example of notes and links in one working surface.

content.text: Obsidian is one surface for the method: the note stays readable while links expose connections. Another approved note app can do the same job with different controls.
If your organisation limits where records can be stored, those rules choose the surface. Do not copy confidential, personal or client material into a new tool merely to complete an exercise.

attrs.alt: A live work question passes through sources, thinking and an output. Useful reasons and decisions fall through a leak unless checked notes are left for the next related job.
attrs.title: Find the knowledge leak before changing the whole system.

content.text: A knowledge leak is the point where useful context becomes hard to find, interpret or reuse. Repair one leak before changing the whole system.
Try it with guidance

Go back to the question you wrote. Draw five columns: source, current location, what it contributes, who can read it, and what becomes difficult later. Add the finished output as a source as well. A decision memo can hide its own reasoning just as easily as a meeting notebook.

For each row, ask four plain questions: could I find this again, could I tell where it came from, could I tell why it mattered, and could the next person use it without asking me? Mark only the first failure in each row. You do not need to score the whole system.

Stop and record: write one sentence in work-leak-map.md in this form. When I need to answer [question], the useful context in [place] becomes hard to [find, interpret or reuse] because [observable reason].
What you will make

Create work-leak-map.md. Include the question, the reader, what they need to do with the answer, the current sources, the leak sentence, and the one leak you will repair. Leave the other problems on the page, marked out of scope.
Try it on your work

Your first map came from memory. Open the real locations now and correct it. Add any source you forgot, delete any source you expected to use but did not, and note whether that changes the leak you chose.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain to a colleague why collecting more notes is not the same as repairing a knowledge leak. Use your map. Do not use the phrase knowledge management.
Try a changed case

A lawyer inherits a matter with a clean folder structure, complete meeting notes and no record of why the previous lawyer rejected one line of argument. Is the leak at capture, during use or at handover? Write down the evidence you would need before you decide.
Check your work
The question is due soon enough to create real pressure, but a poor first attempt is safe to review.
The source list comes from opened files and systems rather than memory alone.
The leak sentence describes an observable failure.
The map names the reader and what they will do with the output next.
One leak is in scope and the rest are parked.
If you get stuck
Start with the last work item that made you search the same places twice.
Write down what a capable colleague would have to ask you before they could carry on.
If the map still covers too much, pick the missing reason behind one recent decision and repair that leak first.

lessons.title: Turn a capture into a source note
lessons.outcome: Convert one real meeting note, highlight or document extract into a source note that preserves the source, your interpretation and the question it can help answer.
lessons.exercise: Take one capture from the work-leak map. Reopen the original source, verify the capture, rewrite the relevant idea in your own words, separate quotation from interpretation, and record the live question the note may help answer.

artifact.description: A checked source note with a precise locator, a short source extract where needed, an explanation in your own words, the question it serves, and any uncertainty or follow-up.

verification: The locator lets another person open the exact source passage, meeting record or data row.
Quoted words and your interpretation are visibly separate.
The note explains why the source matters to the live question instead of merely summarising it.
Uncertainty, missing context and access limits remain visible.
The note does not copy confidential material into an unapproved surface.

content.text: Outcome
Turn one capture into a source note you can inspect later without pretending that copying is the same as understanding.
Before you continue

Choose one highlight, meeting bullet or document extract from your map. Without reopening the source, write what you think it means, where it came from and why it matters. Put a question mark beside anything you cannot verify from memory.
See it

An operations lead writes, Vendor delay caused the incident, in meeting notes. A month later the line looks like a fact. The original incident review says something narrower: a delayed vendor response extended recovery after an internal alert had already been missed. The capture removed the sequence, the internal failure and the difference between cause and duration.

A source note repairs that loss. It keeps the locator, the relevant source words or data, your explanation, and the question the note can help answer. These parts have different authority. The source can support what it actually says. Your explanation can connect it to the work. The question gives the note a reason to exist. Mixing the three produces a neat paragraph whose claims are hard to audit.

Writing in your own words is a check on understanding, not a ban on quotation. Keep exact wording when it matters, such as a contract clause or a stated decision. Label it and give a locator. Then explain what you think it means. If you cannot explain it without copying the sentence again, you have found work to do rather than a note to polish.
A source note has five parts

attrs.alt: Five stacked parts of a source note: source and locator, exact extract, explanation in your own words, live use, and the next check.
attrs.title: Keep the source, exact extract and your interpretation visibly separate.

content.text: The source, the exact extract and your interpretation carry different authority. Keep them visibly separate.
Source: title, author or owner, date, and a locator precise enough to reopen the evidence.
Extract: the smallest quotation, number, image reference or meeting decision needed for the point.
Your words: what the extract means in this context, including any boundary or uncertainty.
Use: the live question or decision this may inform.
Next check: what you still need to verify, compare or ask.
Try it with guidance

Reopen your chosen source. Start with the locator, because every other part depends on being able to inspect the original again. If the source is a meeting, link the agenda or record and name the date and participants. If no record exists, label the note as your recollection and add the person who can confirm it.

Copy only the words or data whose exact form matters. Below that, write two sentences without looking at the source: what this says, and what it does not say. Reopen the source and correct both. Then write one sentence beginning, This matters to my question because. Delete any sentence that merely repeats the extract.
Stop and record: mark each statement in source-note.md as source, interpretation or open question. If one sentence contains more than one kind, split it.
What you will make

Create source-note.md with the five parts above. Give it a title that states the useful point, not the source title. A title such as Delayed vendor response extended recovery is easier to reuse than Incident review notes.
Try it on your work

Use a source that matters to the question you chose. Ask whether your first memory matched the original. Record the correction if it did not. That correction is evidence that the source note did useful work before it became part of any system.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain the difference between a capture, a source extract and a source note. Include one reason a short note can be more trustworthy than a long summary.
Try a changed case

A lawyer has an exact quotation from an authority, but the database link requires a licence the next reader may not have. What belongs in the source note, what belongs in the handover, and what must not be copied? Write the boundary before you decide how much text to retain.
Check your work
The source can be reopened at the exact place that supports the note.
Quotation, interpretation and open questions cannot be mistaken for each other.
The title states the point the note may contribute.
The use sentence connects the note to the live question.
Access and confidentiality limits are recorded.
If you get stuck
Use one paragraph, one meeting decision or one spreadsheet row rather than a whole document.
Write, The source says, I think this means, and I still need to check as temporary labels.
If you still cannot explain the point, ask what decision would change if the source were false. Start there.

sections.title: Make notes reusable
sections.outcome: Decide what job a note must do, then write one useful idea so it can survive outside the task that produced it.

lessons.title: Give each note one job
lessons.outcome: Classify a real note by the job it must do next, then remove the material that belongs in a different kind of note.
lessons.exercise: Take one mixed note from your current work. Decide whether its next job is capture, source evidence, a reusable concept, or a project decision. Keep that job and move or link the rest rather than inventing a large taxonomy.

artifact.description: A before-and-after note with its chosen job, the decision rule used, and a short record of what was removed, moved or linked because it served another job.

verification: The chosen job describes what the note must help someone do next.
The note no longer mixes raw capture, source evidence, reusable explanation and project status without labels.
Material moved elsewhere remains reachable through a link or locator.
The decision did not require a new folder tree or a complete taxonomy.
The note has a clear condition for deletion, update or reuse.

content.text: Outcome
Give one note one clear job, so you can tell what belongs in it and what should move.
Before you continue

Open a note you keep returning to. Without editing it, write the next action it should make easier. Then mark each paragraph as capture, source, idea or project. If a paragraph needs two labels, leave both visible.
See it

An analyst has one page called Pricing research. It contains copied passages, meeting dates, a half-written recommendation, questions for finance, a list of competitors and three tasks. The page feels valuable because it contains everything. It is difficult to use for the same reason. A reader cannot tell which sentences are evidence, which are the analyst's view, or which were only temporary reminders.

The repair is not a more elaborate label. Decide what the note must do next. A capture holds something briefly until you process it. A source note preserves inspectable evidence and your reading of it. A concept note explains one reusable idea. A project or decision note coordinates a live piece of work. These are working jobs, not permanent species. A capture can become a source note. A project decision can later produce a reusable concept.

One-job notes reduce ambiguity at the moment of use. They also give you a reason to split. If the copied evidence must remain inspectable and the recommendation must be edited for an audience, those activities pull in different directions. Link the notes so the relationship remains visible. Do not force both into one page because they arrived on the same afternoon.
Choose by the next use

attrs.alt: A decision guide chooses a note's job from its next use: temporary capture, inspectable source evidence, reusable concept, or live project and decision record.
attrs.title: Choose the note's job from what it must help someone do next.

content.text: Choose a note's job from what it must help someone do next, not from where the note came from.
Need to remember or process it soon: capture.
Need to inspect what a source supports: source note.
Need to reuse an explanation beyond the current project: concept note.
Need to coordinate a current decision, deadline or handover: project or decision note.
If the next use is unclear, keep the note as a capture and give it a review date. Promoting every fragment into a permanent note creates maintenance work before value.
Try it with guidance

Use the note you marked. Write four possible next uses beside it. Cross out any that are hypothetical. Choose the one connected to your live course question. Now read each block of the note and ask whether it directly serves that use.

Keep the blocks that serve the job. For the rest, choose move, link or delete. Move source material into source-note.md. Link a useful concept you need to preserve. Delete temporary reminders that are complete. If you move material, leave a short relation such as supports, contradicts or resulted in. A bare related link postpones the same interpretation problem.
Stop and record: at the top of note-job-decision.md, write, This note exists to help [person] do [next use]. Then list every block you moved and the reason.
What you will make

Create note-job-decision.md with a copy or link to the original note, the chosen job, the before-and-after structure, and a small move log. The log is evidence that the decision changed the note rather than merely adding a label.
Try it on your work

Apply the same test to one meeting note. Do not automatically turn it into minutes. Ask whether its next use is to preserve a decision, support a source claim, coordinate actions or develop an idea. Keep only the form the next use needs.
Teach it back

Close the lesson and explain why note jobs are better chosen by next use than by where the note came from. Give one case where a meeting note should become a source note and one where it should remain a project note.
Try a changed case

A compliance team keeps a decision log that includes exact policy extracts, commentary, approver names and follow-up tasks. Splitting everything would make the audit trail harder to follow. Choose the note's primary job and show how labels or linked source records can preserve the necessary record without applying the one-job rule mechanically.
Check your work
The next use is real and named.
A reader can distinguish source evidence from your view.
Moved material remains reachable.
The note changed in response to its job.
No new taxonomy was created for a single case.
If you get stuck
Ask what you expect to do immediately after opening the note.
If two actions compete, duplicate the title on a blank page and split the blocks between the two jobs.
If neither note is useful after the split, keep the original as a project record and stop.

lessons.title: Write one idea so it can stand alone
lessons.outcome: Write one concept note that states a useful claim, its boundary and its evidence clearly enough to reuse outside the project that produced it.
lessons.exercise: Extract one reusable idea from a source or project note. Give it a claim title, explain it without relying on the original meeting or project, show its evidence and limits, and test it against a second professional case.

artifact.description: One reusable concept note with a claim title, a plain explanation, source links, a boundary or counterexample, and a short test against a second case.

verification: The title is a claim or decision rule rather than a topic label.
The note makes sense without the meeting, project or source page open.
Evidence and interpretation remain distinguishable.
A boundary or counterexample prevents the idea from becoming an absolute rule.
The second case tests the idea rather than merely repeating the first example.

content.text: Outcome
Write one idea so it remains understandable and useful after the project that produced it has moved on.
Before you continue

Pick one sentence from your source or project notes that you expect to use again. Write a title for it. Then ask what a reader would have to know from the original project before that title made sense. List the missing context.
See it

A month-end note says, Check invoices before reporting this variance. Inside the original close, everyone knows which invoices and why. Outside it, the note is a reminder without a reusable idea. The useful concept is more precise: late invoices can make a timing variance look like a cost change, so verify the posting period before explaining the movement.

A concept note states one idea that can travel. One idea does not mean one sentence or one fact. It means one claim, decision rule or explanation that a reader can evaluate as a unit. The note may need a short example, evidence and a boundary. It should not also contain the whole project history, a task list and three unrelated observations.

The title carries much of the load. Cost variance is a topic. Verify posting period before treating a late invoice as a cost change is a usable claim. A good claim title lets search return a possible answer rather than another container to open. It can still be wrong. The body shows when it applies and what supports it.
Make the idea portable, not context-free

attrs.alt: A mixed project note is separated into a source note, one reusable concept and a live decision record, with links preserving how the parts affect each other.
attrs.title: Split a mixed note by job, then link the parts.

content.text: Split by job, then link the parts. The reusable concept keeps one claim, its evidence and its boundary.

Portability does not mean stripping away every proper noun and detail. Domain knowledge often lives in the exception. Record the trigger, the reason and the boundary. A note that says Always reconcile before reporting is too broad to guide action. A note that says Reconcile transactions recorded after the reporting cut-off before explaining a timing variance preserves the condition that makes the rule useful.
Claim: the idea or decision rule in one sentence.
Reason: why it matters and what goes wrong without it.
Evidence: the source note, case or observation that supports it.
Boundary: when it does not apply or what remains uncertain.
Use: a second case where the idea changes a decision.
Try it with guidance

Use the sentence you chose. Rewrite the title as a complete claim with a condition and an action or consequence. Explain the claim to a capable colleague who was not in the original project. Every time you use words such as this, it or they, ask whether the referent survives outside the project.

Link the source note that supports the claim. Add one sentence beginning, This does not mean. Then choose a second case from another client, month, team or type of work. Write what would have to be true before the concept could guide that case.
Stop and record: cover the body and read only the title. Write the action a reader would take. If that action is vague or larger than the evidence supports, repair the title.
What you will make

Create concept-note.md with the claim title, reason, evidence, boundary and second-case test. Keep the source note separate and linked. The concept note should explain the idea, not reproduce the source.
Try it on your work

Ask someone who understands the work but did not see the source to read the note. Let them state when they would use it. Record where their interpretation differs from yours. Repair the note only where the disagreement reveals missing context or an unsupported claim.
Teach it back
Close the note and explain why one idea is not the same as one sentence. Include the purpose of the claim title, the source link and the boundary.
Try a changed case

An operations rule applies only during a particular supplier contract, but the underlying reason may matter elsewhere. Decide what belongs in the reusable concept and what must remain in the contract-specific note. Show how the link preserves the exception without hiding it.
Check your work
The title states a claim with enough condition to guide action.
The body can be understood without the original project open.
The supporting source is reachable.
The boundary prevents an absolute reading.
The second case changes something about how the idea is applied.
If you get stuck
Start the title with a verb such as check, separate, record or compare.
Write the smallest case where the idea is true and the nearest case where it fails.
If the note still contains two decisions, duplicate it and let each copy keep one claim.

sections.title: Connect as the work demands
sections.outcome: Use metadata and links for distinct jobs, then search the existing system before adding another note.

lessons.title: Use tags, properties and links for different jobs
lessons.outcome: Choose whether a real relationship should be expressed as a tag, a property or a link, and write the relationship so the next reader does not have to infer it.
lessons.exercise: Take the source and concept notes you created. Add only the grouping tags, typed properties and narrative links that change how you can find, interpret or maintain them, then record why each connection uses that mechanism.

artifact.description: A small relationship map showing which real connections are groups, typed fields or narrated links, plus the maintenance reason for each one.

verification: Each tag groups notes that you expect to retrieve together.
Each property stores a consistently named field whose value you expect to query, sort or check.
Each link states the relationship in the surrounding sentence or label.
No connection exists only to make the graph or database look full.
A reader can follow the route from source to concept to live question.

content.text: Outcome
Use tags, properties and links for different jobs, so every connection tells you what it is for.
Before you continue
Look at your source note and concept note. Write three relationships you may need later. For each, predict whether you would use a tag, a property or a link. Do not change the notes yet.
See it

A lawyer's matter note has tags for client, research, urgent, contract, handover and Sarah. It also links to three authorities and a decision log. The tags are doing several different jobs: subject, status, person and document type. The links show that pages are related but not whether an authority supports, limits or contradicts the proposed position.

A cleaner system gives each mechanism a role. Tags group notes into useful working sets. Properties store named facts such as matter, owner, status or review date. Links narrate relationships between ideas, evidence and decisions. The body sentence does the important work: Authority A limits the definition used in Concept B tells the reader more than a naked link under Related.

attrs.alt: The OneNote for Windows Insert ribbon with the Link command outlined at the far right.
attrs.title: Find the Link command in OneNote for Windows.

content.text: In OneNote for Windows, select the material you want to connect, then use Insert > Link. The control is different; the job is still to leave a route back to a source or related page.

This distinction is a method, not a law of software. Some tools call every field a property. Some have links without backlinks. Plain files may express a property in a short header. Use the closest available form. What matters is that grouping, typing and reasoning do not collapse into one pile of labels.
Decide from the question the connection must answer

attrs.alt: Three rows show the different jobs of connections: tags group notes, properties store typed fields, and links narrate how one idea affects another.
attrs.title: Tags group, properties type, and links narrate.

content.text: Tags group. Properties type. Links narrate. Keep a connection only when it changes retrieval, interpretation or action.
Which notes should appear together? Use a tag or saved search.
What named field should be checked or filtered consistently? Use a property.
How does this idea or source affect that one? Use a link inside a sentence that names the relationship.

A relationship earns maintenance when it changes retrieval, interpretation or action. A tag you never search, a property nobody checks and a link that says only related are decoration. Leave them out until the work asks for them.
Try it with guidance

Return to your three predicted relationships. Write the question each must answer. If the question starts which notes, test a tag. If it starts what value or who owns, test a property. If it starts how or why, write a link sentence. Change your prediction where the question points elsewhere.

Add one of each only if your notes need it. For the link, use a relationship verb such as supports, contradicts, qualifies, resulted in or replaces. Open the target and add the reverse explanation only when it helps the target's reader. Backlinks show that a link exists; they do not explain its meaning.
Stop and record: in relationship-map.md, list each connection as source, mechanism, target or value, and the question it answers. Remove one connection that cannot answer a real question.
What you will make
Create relationship-map.md. A table is enough. Include the two notes, the live question, the mechanism you chose, the visible wording and the reason it will be maintained.
Try it on your work

Use your chosen tool to retrieve the notes through the connection. Search the tag, filter or inspect the property, and follow the link sentence. Record which mechanism worked and which required you to remember hidden context. Repair only the failing connection.
Teach it back
With the lesson closed, explain the three jobs in one example from your work. Include why a backlink is not the same as a narrated relationship.
Try a changed case

An operations team uses a shared spreadsheet that has columns and filters but no note-to-note links. Show how you would express grouping, typed fields and a narrative relationship without changing tools. Decide what belongs in the spreadsheet and what belongs in a linked decision record.
Check your work
Every tag has a retrieval use.
Every property has a stable name and an owner or review trigger.
Every link names how the notes affect each other.
The route from evidence to concept to question can be followed.
At least one decorative connection was removed or consciously rejected.
If you get stuck
Start with the question you expect to type into search next week.
If a label could mean status, topic or owner, turn it into one named property.
If a link feels vague, finish the sentence: This note changes that note because.

lessons.title: Search before creating
lessons.outcome: Search the existing system for a real idea, compare the candidates, and choose to update, merge, link, archive or create with evidence for the choice.
lessons.exercise: Before adding a new note for the live question, search titles, body text, tags and likely synonyms. Read the best candidates fully, then make and record one update, merge, link, archive or create decision.

artifact.description: A search record with the query variants, candidate notes, comparison, chosen action and the exact change made to the existing system.

verification: The search uses at least one synonym or domain term beyond the intended new title.
The best candidates were read rather than judged from titles or snippets.
The action is one of update, merge, link, archive or create and has a concrete reason.
Creation is used only when no existing note can carry the idea without becoming misleading.
The chosen action leaves the live question easier to answer.
sourceNotes: Knowledge Bank as Agent Working Memory.md

content.text: Outcome
Search before creating, then choose the smallest change that makes the existing knowledge more useful.
Before you continue
Write the title of the next note you expect to create. Predict how many notes in your current system already touch the idea. List three other words a colleague might use for the same thing.
See it

An operations lead is about to create a note called Escalation rules. Search finds Incident severity, Customer communication and On-call handover. Each contains part of the intended rule, with different dates and owners. A fourth note would make the search results look richer while leaving the disagreement unresolved.

Read-before-create turns creation into a fallback. Search titles and body text. Use synonyms. Read each plausible candidate. Then choose an action: update the current note when the idea belongs there; merge when two notes claim the same job; link when both jobs remain useful; archive when a stale note misleads; create when the idea is genuinely distinct.

The important step is comparison, not search volume. A title match can hide a different claim. A note with an old date may still contain the best reasoning. A note with no matching words may describe the same decision in the language of another team. Read enough to compare job, claim, evidence, owner and update state.
Five actions, one decision

attrs.alt: A search and read step leads to a decision: change an existing note by updating, merging, linking or archiving, or create only when no existing note can carry the idea clearly.
attrs.title: Search and read before deciding whether to change or create.

content.text: Creation is the fallback. Search and read first, then make the smallest change that leaves the system more useful.
Update when an existing note has the right job and needs better evidence, wording or state.
Merge when two notes make the same claim or coordinate the same decision.
Link when the notes have different jobs and the relationship matters.
Archive when keeping the note in normal search would mislead a reader.
Create when no candidate can absorb the idea without changing its job or claim.
A system that accretes is not one that only grows. It becomes more useful through correction, consolidation and removal as well as addition.
Try it with guidance

Search the title you predicted. Search the three synonyms. Search one phrase from the source note and one relationship from your map. Put the first five plausible candidates into a small table with title, job, claim, last checked and likely action.

Open the candidates. Do not decide from the snippet. Compare the part that overlaps your intended note. If the notes disagree, keep both until you can identify whether the conflict comes from time, context, evidence or an actual difference in judgement.

Stop and record: choose one action in existing-note-decision.md and complete it now. Paste the before state or locator, the reason, and the after state. If you choose create, name the closest candidate and explain why updating it would make its job less clear.
What you will make
Create existing-note-decision.md with your query variants, candidate comparison, action and changed state. The artifact is not a search log alone. It must show what changed in the system.
Try it on your work

Repeat the search using the vocabulary of another role. If you are in finance, search the operations term for the same event. If you are in law, search the client's words as well as the legal term. Record whether the second vocabulary finds a note your first search missed.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain why search-before-create is not a rule against new notes. Name the evidence that justifies each of the five actions.
Try a changed case

A lawyer finds two advice notes on the same issue for different jurisdictions. Their titles and conclusions look similar. Decide whether to merge, link or keep them separate. State the professional and source checks that must happen before any edit.
Check your work
Search covered titles, body text and alternative vocabulary.
Candidates were read in full where their claims overlap.
The action matches the candidate's job and claim.
A source or owner conflict remains visible rather than being silently resolved.
The system changed in a way the live question can use.
If you get stuck
Search a phrase from the source rather than the title you planned.
Compare only the best two candidates across job, claim and date.
If the action is still unclear, link the candidates with a conflict note and postpone consolidation until the live work resolves it.

sections.title: Think on the page
sections.outcome: Separate discovery from presentation, then combine the notes that matter into an answer to one live question.

lessons.title: Write to discover what you think
lessons.outcome: Use a rough private draft to expose a gap, contradiction or decision before you begin writing for the final reader.
lessons.exercise: Write a short private response to the live question using the sources and concepts you have. Mark claims, evidence, assumptions, conflicts and missing information before doing any audience or style pass.

artifact.description: A rough discovery draft that states the current answer, marks evidence and assumptions, surfaces at least one gap or contradiction, and records the decision that follows.

verification: The draft was written before choosing a polished structure for the final reader.
Claims, evidence, assumptions and questions can be distinguished.
At least one gap or contradiction changed the current answer or next check.
The draft names the decision the writer is trying to make.
Unresolved material remains visible instead of being edited into certainty.
sourceNotes: Write Notes for Yourself by Default, Disregarding Audience.md

content.text: Outcome
Use a rough draft to find what you think before you spend effort making it presentable.
Before you continue
Answer your live question in five sentences without opening your notes. Underline the sentence you trust least. Write what evidence would make you change it.
See it

An analyst is asked whether to renew a supplier contract. She begins with a slide outline: recommendation, benefits, risks, next steps. The structure looks finished before the reasoning has started. When she writes a private page instead, she notices that the strongest service data covers only the period before a staffing change, while the recent complaints cover a different product tier. The apparent trend combines two populations.

Discovery writing has a different reader from presentation writing. Its first reader is the person doing the thinking. It can be repetitive, uncertain and badly ordered because its job is to expose what you believe, what supports it and where it breaks. Presentation writing serves somebody else. It chooses sequence, emphasis and form after the reasoning can survive inspection.

Trying to do both at once creates a quiet conflict. The need to sound clear encourages you to smooth over uncertainty just when uncertainty is most useful. The need to choose a structure encourages you to stop searching once each heading has something under it. Separate the passes. Discovery can be private. Evidence and professional duties still apply.
Use marks that expose the draft

attrs.alt: A private discovery-writing pass exposes claims, evidence, assumptions, missing information and decisions before a separate presentation pass orders the answer for a reader.
attrs.title: Discovery writing and presentation writing are separate passes.

content.text: Discovery writing finds the thought. Presentation writing arranges the checked reasoning for another person.
[C] for a claim you expect the output to make.
[E] for the source or observation that supports it.
[A] for an assumption or professional judgement.
[?] for missing information or a contradiction.
[D] for the decision or action the paragraph implies.
These marks are temporary. Their value is the mismatch they reveal. A claim with no evidence, three sources with no decision, or a decision built entirely on judgement tells you what to inspect next.
Try it with guidance

Set a short boundary: one page or the current question, not everything you know. Write the answer you currently believe. Add a reason after every major claim. When a source disagrees, place the disagreement beside the claim rather than in a later concerns section.

Apply the five marks. Follow the weakest sentence from your prediction. Open the relevant source and concept notes. Correct the draft, but do not polish it. At the bottom, write what changed and what evidence caused the change.

Stop and record: write one sentence beginning, I started by thinking, and a second beginning, The evidence changed this because. If nothing changed, record the strongest unresolved question and the source that would answer it.
What you will make
Create thinking-draft.md with the rough answer, the five marks, the changed view and the remaining question. Do not delete the false start. It is part of the evidence for how the decision developed.
Try it on your work

Give the draft a private title that states the question. Search your notes for one piece of evidence that would make your preferred answer less comfortable. Add it beside the relevant claim and decide whether it changes the conclusion, the confidence or the next action.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain the different jobs of discovery writing and presentation writing. Name one thing that should stay in the private draft and one thing the final reader must still see.
Try a changed case

A senior lawyer already knows the likely answer and has limited time. Show how a short discovery pass can test the weakest premise without turning into a long essay. State which professional checks cannot be replaced by the writing exercise.
Check your work
The current answer appears before the polished outline.
Claims and evidence can be paired.
Judgement and missing evidence remain labelled.
A contradiction or gap changed the answer, confidence or next check.
The draft ends with a decision or an explicit unresolved question.
If you get stuck
Write the answer you hope is true, then ask what would disprove it.
Put [C], [E] or [?] at the start of every paragraph before changing any prose.
If the page still feels blank, explain the question in an email to yourself and keep the first sentence that surprises you.

lessons.title: Build a synthesis note around a live question
lessons.outcome: Combine only the sources, concepts and conflicts that change one live question, then state the answer, uncertainty and next decision in a synthesis note.
lessons.exercise: Create a synthesis hub for the course question. Pull in the source and concept notes that change the answer, group them by the reasoning they contribute, preserve conflicts, and write the current answer and next decision at the top.

artifact.description: A question-led synthesis note with the current answer, grouped evidence and concepts, visible disagreements, implications, open checks and a next decision.

verification: The title is the live question rather than a broad topic.
Every included note changes the answer, uncertainty or next action.
Conflicting sources or concepts remain visible and are not averaged into vague prose.
The synthesis distinguishes evidence, interpretation and judgement.
The top section states the current answer and what must happen next.
sourceNotes: Create Speculative Outlines While You Write.md

content.text: Outcome
Build one synthesis note that answers a live question without becoming an index of everything related to the topic.
Before you continue

Write your current answer to the course question in one sentence. Under it, list the three notes you expect to matter most and the change each one should make to the answer. Mark any note you are including only because it looks related.
See it

An operations lead builds an incident knowledge page. It links every alert, meeting, action item, supplier note and policy. The page is complete but cannot answer the live question: should the team change the escalation threshold? The useful synthesis needs only the evidence about missed signals, false alarms, response cost and who can act. Everything else may remain linked elsewhere.

A synthesis note is organised around a question and the reasoning needed to answer it. It does not replace source notes or concept notes. It uses them. Its job is to make their relationship visible: this evidence supports the threshold change, that case limits it, this concept explains why the false alarms matter, and this missing number blocks a final decision.

The shape can be temporary. A speculative outline is useful because it gives new evidence somewhere to land. Change the headings when the reasoning changes. If the first structure was wrong, that is not a failure. A synthesis that never changes may be organising sources after the fact rather than helping you think.
A small synthesis has six parts

attrs.alt: Sources, concepts and visible conflicts feed one live question. The synthesis produces a current answer, an open check and the next decision.
attrs.title: Build a synthesis around one live question, not a topic index.

content.text: A note belongs in the synthesis only when it changes the answer, uncertainty or next action.
Question: the decision or uncertainty the note exists to resolve.
Current answer: one direct sentence, with confidence or boundary where needed.
Reasoning groups: headings that express the parts of the argument, not source categories.
Conflict: sources, concepts or interests that point in different directions.
Open checks: evidence that could change the answer.
Next decision: what someone should decide, ask or do now.

Surprise is a useful check. The synthesis should reveal at least one relationship, condition or disagreement that was not visible in the source list. If it merely repeats each note in sequence, group by the reasoning instead.
Try it with guidance

Put the live question at the top. Paste your one-sentence answer below it. Bring in the three predicted notes, but link them rather than copying their full contents. For each, write the relationship to the answer. Remove any note that cannot finish the sentence, This changes the answer by.

Add one note or source that pushes against the current answer. Create headings from the tension you now see. In the supplier example, the headings might be Missed signals, Cost of false alarms and Authority to act. Those headings organise reasoning. Source types such as Meetings and Documents do not.

Stop and record: rewrite the current answer after arranging the evidence. Add a short change note: I expected, the synthesis showed, so the next decision is. If the answer did not change, record the new boundary or confidence instead.
What you will make
Create synthesis-hub.md with the six parts. Keep links and locators to the notes. The hub is an argument map for one question, not a duplicate archive.
Try it on your work

Ask a colleague to read only the question, current answer and headings. Let them predict the reasoning. If their prediction misses a material issue, rename or reorder the headings. Then let them follow one source link and check whether the relationship sentence is fair.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain how a synthesis note differs from a folder, index and summary. Name the test that decides whether a note belongs in the synthesis.
Try a changed case

An accountant's question is whether a variance needs escalation. The source notes agree on the number but disagree on whether it is timing or a real cost change. Build the smallest synthesis structure that preserves the disagreement and identifies the check that would resolve it.
Check your work
The title can be answered, not merely explored.
The current answer is direct and bounded.
Every included note changes the reasoning.
Conflict and missing evidence remain visible.
The synthesis ends with a decision or check.
If you get stuck
Turn the topic into, What should we decide about this now?
Keep only the three notes that most change your answer.
If the structure is still a source list, write supports, limits or contradicts beside every link and group by those effects.

sections.title: Work with AI from checked notes
sections.outcome: Choose the notes an AI tool is allowed to use, then check every proposed change before it becomes part of the knowledge system.

lessons.title: Give AI a source pack, not your whole archive
lessons.outcome: Turn a live question and a small set of checked notes into a bounded AI work brief with explicit exclusions, source locators and a stop condition.
lessons.exercise: Choose one low-risk question from your synthesis, select only the notes needed to answer it, record why each note belongs, state what the AI may do, and keep confidential or irrelevant material outside the source pack.

artifact.description: A bounded brief containing the job, selected sources, exact locators, allowed use, exclusions, output shape and the condition that should stop the AI rather than let it guess.

verification: The brief names one job and one reader rather than asking the AI to understand the whole archive.
Every included note changes the answer, supplies evidence or states a necessary constraint.
Each source has a locator that a reviewer can open without searching the entire system.
Excluded material and organisational storage rules are written down before any upload or connection.
The stop condition tells the AI what missing evidence must cause a question or refusal.
sourceNotes: Knowledge Bank as Agent Working Memory.md

content.text: Outcome
Give an AI tool enough checked context to do one job without handing it a whole archive and hoping it finds the right boundaries.
Before you continue
Choose the live question from your synthesis. Before reading on, write which notes you would give the AI and which you would keep out. Beside each choice, write the reason. Do not open the tool yet.
See it

An operations lead wants help drafting a decision note after a supplier incident. Her knowledge system contains the incident timeline, two meeting notes, the current escalation rule, last year's supplier review, an unrelated complaint, personal contact details and an old rule that has since changed. Asking an AI tool to read everything feels thorough. It also hides the most important decisions: which rule is current, which evidence belongs to this incident and which material the tool should never receive.

She makes a source pack instead. It contains the incident timeline, the exact section of the current escalation rule and the meeting decisions that changed the next action. Each item has a locator and a one-line reason for inclusion. The old rule stays outside the pack, but the brief warns that an older version exists. Personal details are removed because the draft does not need them.

The pack does not make the AI correct. It makes the job inspectable. A colleague can see what the tool was allowed to use, notice a missing source and reproduce the draft with the same boundary. A whole archive makes those decisions implicit. The model then has to guess which document is current, which note is evidence and which text is only background.
Treat context as a working boundary

attrs.alt: A job contract filters a larger archive into a small AI source pack. Current, relevant and permitted notes enter; stale, unrelated and restricted notes stay outside.
attrs.title: Choose a checked source pack for one AI job.

content.text: Start with the job. Include only current, relevant and permitted sources, and write down what stays outside. The boundary is evidence, not a guarantee.

Good working context answers six questions: What is the job? Who will use the result? Which sources may support it? What is explicitly out? What shape should the answer take? When should the AI stop and ask? These are job decisions, not prompt decoration.

Use only a tool and storage location your organisation permits. A source pack is not permission to move client, employee, financial or confidential material into a new service. If the approved tool cannot receive the needed sources, do the exercise with public or synthetic material and record the boundary.
Try it with guidance
Write the job before you choose the notes. Use one sentence with a verb, an object and a reader: Draft a two-page exception brief for the finance reviewer. Then work through the source list.
Copy the live question and name the person who will use the answer.
For each candidate note, finish: This belongs because it changes the answer, supplies evidence or sets a constraint.
Add the exact page, heading, paragraph, row or date that lets another person find the source.
Write the allowed use and output shape. Drafting, comparison and question-finding are different jobs.
List exclusions and write the missing-source condition that must stop the work.
Stop and record: remove one note from the pack. If the expected answer does not change, the note was background rather than working context. Record the removal and why it was safe.
What you will make

Create ai-source-brief.md. Include the job, reader, selected source list with locators, reason for each source, allowed use, output shape, exclusions and stop condition. Keep the file beside the synthesis it came from.
Try it on your work

Run the brief on the lowest-risk version of your question. Ask the AI to name which supplied source supports each material claim and to mark any gap instead of filling it. Save the response as a draft outside your trusted notes. Do not let the tool write back to the source notes yet.

If your organisation does not permit this use, run the same brief against public documents or a small synthetic case. The learning target is the boundary and the evidence path, not access to a particular product.
Teach it back

Close the lesson and explain why a smaller checked source pack is better than a whole archive for one bounded job. Include the privacy boundary, the reviewer and the condition that should make the AI stop.
Try a changed case

Your approved AI tool cannot open internal links. A colleague offers to paste the full contents of every linked page into one document. Decide what should be copied, summarised, excluded or replaced with a locator. Preserve enough source identity that the resulting claims can still be checked.
Check your work
The job, reader and output shape are specific enough to tell when the work is done.
Every selected source has a reason and a locator.
No confidential or irrelevant material entered the pack merely because it was nearby.
The brief distinguishes source facts, your judgement and the AI's proposed wording.
The stop condition exposes missing evidence instead of rewarding a plausible guess.
If you get stuck
Start with the reader. What must they decide after reading the answer?
Keep a source only if removing it changes a claim, constraint or uncertainty.
Use this stop condition: If the supplied sources do not support a material claim, name the missing evidence and do not complete that part.

lessons.title: Review the answer before it joins your notes
lessons.outcome: Compare an AI draft with its source pack, decide what to accept, repair or reject, and update trusted notes only after the evidence and decision are visible.
lessons.exercise: Take one low-risk AI draft made from your source brief, check each material claim against the supplied sources, label every proposed note change accept, repair or reject, and record the reason before updating anything trusted.

artifact.description: A claim-by-claim review showing the proposed change, supporting source, decision, repair or rejection reason, and the exact trusted note that may be updated after review.

verification: Every material claim is compared with a source from the approved pack.
Accepted wording is separated from the source text and from the reviewer's judgement.
Repairs and rejections record a concrete reason rather than a confidence score.
No trusted note is updated before the review decision is recorded.
The final note keeps uncertainty or exceptions that could change later use.
sourceNotes: Knowledge Bank as Agent Working Memory.md

content.text: Outcome
Treat an AI answer as a proposed change. Check it against the source pack before any sentence becomes part of a trusted note, synthesis or brief.
Before you continue

Read the AI draft once without opening the sources. Mark the sentences that feel most convincing. Predict which sentences you would allow back into your notes and which one deserves the slowest check. Record the prediction before continuing.
See it

A lawyer uses a checked source pack to draft a matter handover. The answer is clear and mostly faithful. One sentence says the client approved the proposed timetable. The meeting note says the client was comfortable with the direction but wanted to see dates first. Another paragraph combines the current authority with an older internal note and quietly drops the jurisdiction named in the source.

Nothing in the draft looks absurd. That is why fluency is a weak review signal. The useful question is not whether the answer sounds professional. It is whether each material sentence keeps the authority, boundary and uncertainty of the source it relies on.

The lawyer creates a change review. The timetable sentence is rejected because it turns a conditional response into approval. The authority paragraph is repaired to restore the jurisdiction. A concise description of the next meeting is accepted because the date and purpose match the meeting record. Only then are the handover notes updated.
Use decisions, not confidence scores

attrs.alt: Each material claim in an AI draft is compared with the checked source pack, then accepted, repaired and checked again, or rejected. Only reviewed changes return to the notes.
attrs.title: Review an AI draft before it rejoins the notes.

content.text: Accept, repair or reject each material claim. Only supported or repaired-and-rechecked wording may return to the notes.

Accept means the source supports the claim and the wording preserves its boundary. Repair means the underlying point is useful but the wording, scope or source link must change. Reject means the source pack does not support the claim or the claim does not belong in the trusted note. These decisions leave a review trail another person can inspect.

The review should improve the source system as well as the draft. If checking the draft against a current source shows that a concept note is stale, update or supersede that note. If the source pack omitted a current rule, fix the pack. If the brief allowed guessing, repair the stop condition. The checked discrepancy shows where the setup needs repair.
Try it with guidance
Compare each material claim with the source pack. Work in a table with five columns: proposed claim, source locator, decision, reason, trusted note affected.
Copy one claim at a time. Do not review a whole paragraph as one unit.
Open the cited source and find the exact passage, row or meeting decision.
Choose accept, repair or reject. Write the source-based reason before editing the sentence.
Record whether the draft exposed a stale note, missing source or weak instruction.
Stop and record: find the sentence you originally marked as most convincing. Compare your first impression with the source-based decision. Write what the difference reveals about your review habit.
What you will make

Create change-review.md. Include the draft version or date, one row for every material claim, the exact source locator, accept, repair or reject, the reason, and any source note or instruction that must change.
Try it on your work

Review the draft from the previous lesson. Make the accepted and repaired changes in a working copy first. When the review table and final wording agree, update the relevant concept or synthesis notes. Preserve source extracts, locators and unresolved questions. Do not replace the source note with the AI summary.
Finish by changing one part of the setup. Add a missing locator, narrow the source pack, strengthen the stop condition or mark a stale note as superseded. The next run should inherit the correction.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain why a fluent answer is still only a proposed change. Describe the difference between checking the draft, editing the prose and repairing the knowledge system.
Try a changed case

An AI draft correctly combines two sources but drops an exception that appears in only one of them. The headline recommendation remains true for most cases. Decide whether to accept, repair or reject it, then show where the exception belongs so a later search cannot miss it.
Check your work
Every material claim has a source locator and an explicit decision.
Repairs preserve scope, exceptions and uncertainty from the source.
Rejected claims remain in the review record with the reason they failed.
Trusted notes changed only after the review table was complete.
The source pack or instruction now carries at least one useful correction from the run.
If you get stuck
Start with the sentence that could most change a decision or action.
Underline the exact words in the source that support the claim, then compare scope and certainty.
If you cannot choose, reject the sentence from the trusted note and record the source or professional review still needed.

sections.title: Ship from the system
sections.outcome: Turn the synthesis into a brief for a real reader, then update the notes and handover so the next related job starts with checked context.

lessons.title: Move from notes to an outline and a decision
lessons.outcome: Turn the synthesis into a reader-led outline and a working brief that makes the decision, evidence, uncertainty and next action easy to inspect.
lessons.exercise: Name the reader and decision, arrange the synthesis around what that reader must understand and do, draft the brief from linked evidence, and check every material claim against its source before polishing.

artifact.description: A source-backed brief for one named reader, with the decision or recommendation first, the minimum supporting reasoning, visible uncertainty and a concrete next action.

verification: The opening states the decision, recommendation or answer the reader needs.
Each material claim is supported by a reachable source or labelled as judgement.
The structure follows the reader's decision rather than the order in which notes were created.
Uncertainty that could change the decision remains visible.
The final section names an owner, action or question.
sourceNotes: Evergreen Notes Permit Smooth Incremental Progress in Writing.md

content.text: Outcome
Turn the synthesis into a brief that lets one real reader inspect the answer and act on it.
Before you continue
Write the reader's name or role and the decision they face. List the first three things you expect to put in the brief. Then ask which of those serves your memory rather than their decision.
See it

An analyst's synthesis has six reasoning groups, nine source notes and two unresolved questions. Copying that structure into a report would show the work but make the director reconstruct the decision. The director needs the recommendation, the two reasons that make it credible, the uncertainty that could change it, and the next action. The rest remains available through links.

The route from notes to output is not copy and paste. It is a change of job. Source notes preserve evidence. Concept notes preserve explanations. The synthesis organises reasoning around a question. The brief is for a reader who must decide or act. Its structure begins with that use, even when the writer discovered the answer in a different order.

A speculative outline is the bridge. Write the decision at the top. Add the minimum questions the reader must answer before accepting it. Pull the relevant reasoning from the synthesis under those questions. Keep source links beside claims while drafting. Citation style can wait; traceability cannot.
A working brief can stay small

attrs.alt: Source and concept notes feed a question-led synthesis, which becomes a reader-led outline and then a brief with decision, evidence, boundary and next action.
attrs.title: Each stage changes the job from preserving evidence to helping a reader decide.

content.text: Each stage has a different job. The brief follows the reader's decision, not the order in which the notes were created.
Decision: what you recommend, conclude or need the reader to choose.
Why: the few reasons that materially support it.
Evidence: links or locators beside the claims they support.
Boundary: uncertainty, judgement and evidence that points elsewhere.
Next: the action, owner or question that follows.

This shape is not a universal template. A legal advice outline, month-end review and incident decision note have different formal requirements. Use the required professional form. Keep the source-to-decision path inside it.
Try it with guidance

Write the decision and reader first. Turn each reasoning group in your synthesis into a question the reader may ask. Keep only the questions that could change acceptance, interpretation or action. Arrange them in the order the reader needs, not the order of your research.

Draft from the synthesis, but reopen every material source before finalising the claim. Put the locator beside the sentence. Mark judgement. If the brief says the evidence proves more than the source says, narrow the sentence. If an uncertainty cannot change the decision, move it out of the main path. If it can, keep it visible.

Stop and record: give the brief to the intended reader or a proxy and ask only, What do you think I am asking you to decide or do? Record their answer before explaining. Repair the opening if their answer differs.
What you will make

Create working-brief.md in the required professional form. It must still expose the decision, evidence, uncertainty and next action. Keep the synthesis as the working record rather than forcing every useful detail into the brief.
Try it on your work

Read the draft once as the reader. Hide the source notes. Mark any sentence that asks the reader to trust you without enough evidence or context. Then inspect the linked source and choose add evidence, label judgement, narrow the claim or remove the sentence.
Teach it back
Close the lesson and explain the different jobs of source note, concept note, synthesis and brief. Describe why the brief should not preserve the order in which the research happened.
Try a changed case

A lawyer must produce an advice outline whose formal structure is prescribed. Show where decision, evidence, uncertainty and next action fit without replacing that structure. Name the source and professional checks that remain outside this course.
Check your work
The opening states the answer or decision.
The structure follows the reader's use.
Material claims have checked sources beside them.
Judgement and uncertainty are visible.
The final action, owner or question is concrete.
If you get stuck
Write, I recommend, because, unless and next as temporary headings.
Use one source link per material claim before improving the prose.
If the brief remains long, ask which paragraph would change the reader's decision. Move the rest back to the synthesis.

lessons.title: Close the loop so the next job starts ahead
lessons.outcome: Run the full method on a fresh question, then update the reusable notes and leave a handover with an owner, uncertainty and a trigger for the next check.
lessons.exercise: Run the capstone on a fresh, low-risk work question. Produce the four final files, use the finished brief with its intended reader, then update the source, concept and synthesis notes in response to what the run exposed.

artifact.description: A compact handover from the capstone run recording what was decided, what changed in the notes, what remains uncertain, who owns the next action and what event should trigger a review.

verification: The capstone uses a fresh real question and four final files.
The finished brief was checked with its intended reader or a named proxy.
At least one source, concept or synthesis note changed in response to the run.
The handover names uncertainty, owner and a real review trigger.
A future reader can follow the path from source to decision and see what not to assume.
sourceNotes: Knowledge Bank as Agent Working Memory.md

content.text: Outcome
Use the whole method on a fresh work question, then leave the notes in a better state for the next related job.
Before you continue

Choose a fresh question you already need to answer. Predict which existing note will save you the most work and which note is most likely to be wrong, incomplete or stale. Write both predictions before opening them.
See it

An operations lead finishes an incident brief and files it. The brief solves today's job. The useful work around it can still disappear: the source note may keep a wrong interpretation, the concept note may omit the exception, and the synthesis may continue to show an open question that the incident resolved. Without a closing pass, the next incident begins from a misleading system.

Knowledge accrues when real work leaves checked material behind. That requires more than saving the output. Use exposed gaps to update the notes that fed the work. Record the reason for the change. Add an owner or a trigger for anything that can become stale. Archive the note whose normal search result would now mislead.

A handover closes the loop. It tells the next reader what was decided, what evidence was checked, what remains uncertain and what event should cause a review. It also records what not to infer. A date property without a decision about when or why to revisit the note is decoration.
Capstone: turn notes into useful work

attrs.alt: A loop moves from a fresh work question to a checked brief, then updates the owning notes and records uncertainty, owner and review trigger before the next related job.
attrs.title: Close the loop by updating the notes after the real run.

content.text: The next job starts ahead only when the real run changes the notes and leaves a reason to check them again.
Use one fresh, low-risk question you would have had to answer anyway. The twelve lesson artefacts are your working records. Consolidate or reference them in exactly four final files from this run:
source-pack.md: the checked sources, locators, extracts, interpretations and open checks used in this run.
concept-map.md: the reusable concepts and only the relationships that changed the answer.
working-brief.md: the source-backed answer for the named reader, with uncertainty and next action.
handover.md: what changed during the run, what remains uncertain, the owner and the review trigger.

If you use an approved AI tool on this run, keep ai-source-brief.md and change-review.md as working records, link them from the four final files, and carry their exclusions, claim decisions and unresolved checks into the source pack or handover.

The final files must describe what happened. If a source was missing, record the refusal, workaround or question. If your preferred answer changed, keep the evidence. If the system did not help, record where it failed rather than writing a smoother success story.
Try it with guidance

Start with search-before-create. Reuse or correct existing source and concept notes. Build the synthesis around the fresh question. Draft the working brief for its reader and check every material claim. Use or review the brief with that reader or a named proxy.

After the output is used, inspect the run backwards. Which source note was difficult to verify? Which concept needed a boundary? Which relationship was missing or decorative? Which part of the synthesis did the reader misunderstand? Update the owning note and record the run that caused the change.
Stop and record: compare your two predictions with the run. In handover.md, write what actually saved effort, what proved stale or incomplete, and the first thing the next person should verify.
What you will make

Submit source-pack.md, concept-map.md, working-brief.md and handover.md. The working records can remain separate. The four final files must provide an index and evidence bundle for the fresh run rather than pretending that every setup note was created during it.
Try it on your work

Give the handover and brief to the intended reader or a proxy. Ask them to state the decision, the strongest evidence, the uncertainty and the next check. Record their answer. Repair the files only where the mismatch could change action or trust.
Teach it back

Close every course file. Explain the full loop from live question to source note, concept, relationship, search, discovery draft and synthesis. Then explain how a checked AI source pack and claim review feed the brief and handover when AI use is approved. Name the point where the system could still mislead the next person.
Try a changed case

The next related job arrives after a policy, contract or reporting rule has changed. Decide which note should warn the reader, which source must be reopened and which old conclusion should remain visible as history rather than being silently overwritten.
Check your work
All four final files come from one fresh real run.
The path from source to claim to decision is inspectable.
The reader's understanding was checked.
At least one reusable note changed because of evidence from the run.
The handover names uncertainty, owner and review trigger.
If you get stuck
Choose the smallest real question whose answer still matters to another person.
Use the four final filenames as headings and link the working records under the file that uses them.
If no note changed, ask where the run surprised, delayed or corrected you. Update the note that should have prepared you for that moment.

capstone.title: Capstone: turn notes into useful work
capstone.outcome: Answer one real work question with a source-backed brief, then leave a compact handover that makes the next related job easier to start.
capstone.exercise: Choose a fresh, low-risk question you already need to answer. Use the course method to gather and check the relevant sources, make the important ideas reusable, connect only the relationships the question needs, write the brief, and record what should be updated or reused next time. Submit source-pack.md, concept-map.md, working-brief.md and handover.md as evidence from the run.
verification: The question was real, bounded and safe to use for practice.
Every material claim in the working brief points to a source in source-pack.md or is clearly marked as judgement.
The concept map includes only relationships that changed the analysis, decision or handover.
The working brief answers the question for a named reader and ends with a decision, recommendation or next action.
The handover records what changed during the run, what remains uncertain, and the trigger for checking or updating the notes.
You can explain the path from source to decision with the four files closed.
